A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same neural-collapse-based OOD detector. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR detection experiments, hard-OOD evaluations, loss ablations, feature analyses and repeated-run results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds ImageNet evaluation, architecture comparisons, sensitivity studies and robustness experiments, including appendix results.

M1.justification: The core losses and detection score remain equivalent under renaming. However, v2 Section 3.4 and Appendix A.5 describe cross-entropy-only stage I, whereas v1 Eq. 6 includes OE loss, and explicitly permit skipping stage I for pretrained models. Appendix A.1 also introduces an Energy-OE-based combined objective. These are limited procedural adaptations.

E1.justification: v2 adds ImageNet-1k as an ID benchmark, ImageNet-21k-p auxiliary data, and evaluation against iNaturalist, SUN, Places and Textures. v1 used ImageNet-Resize only as an OOD dataset. v2 also adds Tiny-ImageNet to hard-OOD evaluation and a class-imbalanced CIFAR10-LT scenario, substantially extending coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding CIFAR comparisons retain MSP, Energy, Maha, KNN, CSI, CIDER, KNN+, OE, Energy-OE, POEM and DAL. The existing hard-OOD comparator membership also remains unchanged. Added evaluations reuse existing comparators; the removed loss configuration is an ablation, not a separate baseline method.

E3.justification: v2 introduces ImageNet fine-tuning with five epochs, batch size 64 and learning rate 1e-4; additional ResNet, DenseNet and ViT configurations; coefficient and training-duration sweeps; and ID-accuracy reporting. Original CIFAR numerical hyperparameters remain documented. The revised stage-I loss description is a reported protocol change, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds hyperparameter and training-schedule sensitivity, low-feature-dimension and class-imbalance tests, Energy-OE compatibility, class-mean-based separation analysis, and visualizations covering all CIFAR10 classes. Conversely, the feature-loss-without-OE control in v1 Table 3 disappears from v2 Table 5. Existing stability and scoring analyses are retained in Appendices A.7–A.8.

E5.justification: The five-repetition study reporting means and quantities described as variances is retained unchanged from v1 Table 5 to v2 Table 15. No additional seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests or changed uncertainty-estimation procedures are reported.

E6.justification: Original CIFAR results are retained, including 29.47 FPR95 and 94.00 AUROC on CIFAR100. Substantial new results cover ImageNet, architectures, sensitivity and robustness. In v2 Table 1, ResNet50 achieves 56.73/84.62 versus OE's 59.66/83.89; ViT FPR95 is 56.88 versus DAL's better 56.67. The no-OE ablation results are removed.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds a formal alternative optimization objective combining the energy-margin loss with the proposed clustering and separation terms, particularly Eq. 9. This is a limited extension of the mathematical formulation. The original NC geometry, core loss definitions and detection score remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the claimed state-of-the-art performance from CIFAR benchmarks to include ImageNet. The central contributions—feature separation using auxiliary OOD data, its NC-based construction, and its potential as a stronger training baseline—remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses feature-dimension requirements, failure of NC, and why minority collapse can preserve useful low-dimensional structure. It also explains clustering-only degradation and motivates class-mean measurements to reduce alignment with the training objective. These replace and expand beyond v1 Appendix A.1's practical limitation concerning auxiliary data, fine-tuning and possible test-time adaptation, which is removed.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promised future code release with a reported repository link, documents ImageNet initialization and fine-tuning settings, and explains the visualization projection in Appendix A.9. Existing CIFAR implementation details largely remain. The RTX 4090 hardware disclosure is removed, and some new settings, including the imbalance ratio, remain unspecified.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly contrasts its optimization approach with KNN's fixed-feature scoring and adds references supporting new architectures, datasets, minority collapse and intermediate-layer NC. The test-time-adaptation references accompanying v1's limitation are removed. The central positioning relative to OE and NC-based detection remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: hard-OOD, stability and scoring studies move into the expanded appendix, while architecture and sensitivity sections enter the main text. Limitations become a main section, training and ablation explanations are rewritten, and OrthLoss/LNC become Separation Loss/LClu. Much of the introductory argument remains intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive benchmark, sensitivity and robustness tables plus five multi-panel feature visualizations. It restructures the ablation table from component checkmarks to explicit loss combinations, expands the hard-OOD table, and introduces near/far-OOD grouping. Existing displays are resized and relocated within a substantially reformatted ICLR layout.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence centers on CIFAR and one backbone. v2 substantially strengthens generalizability through ImageNet and multiple architectures, and examines the method's central assumptions through imbalance, feature-dimension and sensitivity studies. Class-mean measurements also provide a less objective-aligned check of feature separation. Removing the no-OE ablation and leaving some new protocols underspecified are drawbacks, but the broader validation and more substantive applicability discussion provide a clear overall quality gain.
